title: NumPy Exponential, Logistic and Chi-Square Distributions
learningObjectives: Explain the concepts behind numpy exponential, logistic and chi-square distributions.
Choose an appropriate NumPy random generator method and its parameters.
Use seeded generators for reproducible examples and tests.
Validate sample shape, range and data type.
Describe the assumptions and limitations of a finite random sample.

understand.concept: NumPy provides additional random distributions for different modeling assumptions. The exponential distribution models non-negative waiting times, the logistic distribution has a location and scale, and the chi-square distribution is defined by degrees of freedom. Parameters describe the model and should be chosen based on the problem rather than adjusted to force a desired sample.
understand.whyItMatters: Knowing several distributions helps learners select a model that matches the quantity and assumptions being simulated.
understand.analogy: A random generator is like a repeatable deck-shuffling machine: a starting seed and the sequence of operations determine the generated sequence.
understand.summary: NumPy provides additional random distributions for different modeling assumptions. explain.narrative: Run the examples and inspect the sample properties. A random sample is not a promise of exact theoretical frequencies; tests should focus on stable properties such as shape, valid range and reproducibility. examples.title: Sample non-negative exponential waiting times
examples.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
x = rng.exponential(scale=2, size=100)
print(bool(np.all(x >= 0)), x.shape)
examples.explanation: This example demonstrates sample non-negative exponential waiting times with a seeded NumPy random generator so the validation is deterministic.

examples.title: Generate logistic samples
examples.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
x = rng.logistic(loc=0, scale=1, size=80)
print(x.shape, bool(np.all(np.isfinite(x))))
examples.explanation: This example demonstrates generate logistic samples with a seeded NumPy random generator so the validation is deterministic.

examples.title: Generate chi-square samples
examples.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
x = rng.chisquare(df=4, size=60)
print(bool(np.all(x >= 0)), x.size)
examples.explanation: This example demonstrates generate chi-square samples with a seeded NumPy random generator so the validation is deterministic.

examples.title: Compare distribution outputs
examples.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
a = rng.exponential(size=25)
b = rng.chisquare(df=3, size=25)
print(a.shape == b.shape, bool(np.all(a >= 0) and np.all(b >= 0)))
examples.explanation: This example demonstrates compare distribution outputs with a seeded NumPy random generator so the validation is deterministic.

examples.title: Validate scale and degrees of freedom
examples.code:
import numpy as np
scale, df = 2.0, 5
assert scale > 0 and df > 0
x = np.random.default_rng(5).chisquare(df=df, size=10)
print(x.size, bool(np.all(x >= 0)))
examples.explanation: This example demonstrates validate scale and degrees of freedom with a seeded NumPy random generator so the validation is deterministic.

practise.guidedTask: Use a seeded NumPy Generator to create a sample relevant to numpy exponential, logistic and chi-square distributions. Print its shape and verify the model's required range or count constraints.
practise.independentTask: Write a small simulation using an appropriate distribution. Explain the model parameters, state the assumptions and add deterministic tests using a fixed seed.
hints: Prefer np.random.default_rng over the legacy global random state.

Check parameter constraints before generating samples.
Distinguish theoretical properties from observed sample statistics.
Use a larger sample only when it serves a clear statistical purpose.
practise.challenge: Compare two appropriate distributions with the same sample size, summarize their assumptions and create a reproducible validation routine.

questions.prompt: What does a seeded NumPy Generator provide?
questions.answer: A reproducible pseudo-random sequence when the generator and call sequence are the same.
options: A truly random sequence that can never repeat.
A reproducible pseudo-random sequence when the generator and call sequence are the same.
A guarantee of exact theoretical frequencies.
A generator that ignores its parameters.
questions.explanation: A seed initializes a deterministic pseudo-random process.

questions.prompt: Why should distribution parameters be chosen carefully?
questions.answer: They encode the assumptions and scale of the model.
options: They encode the assumptions and scale of the model.
They only change the printed format.
They guarantee a fixed sample mean.
They remove the need to validate data.
questions.explanation: Parameters define the distribution being modeled.

questions.prompt: Which check is generally robust for a generated sample?
questions.answer: Check its shape and valid range.
options: Require the sample mean to equal the theoretical mean exactly.
Check its shape and valid range.
Assume every generated value is unique.
Expect the same values from different seeds.
questions.explanation: Shape and support constraints are stable properties.

questions.prompt: What does sampling without replacement mean?
questions.answer: The same population item cannot be selected more than once in that sample.
options: The same population item cannot be selected more than once in that sample.
Every possible item must be selected.
The sample must be sorted.
The generator cannot use a seed.
questions.explanation: Without replacement, selected population members are not repeated.

questions.prompt: What is an important limitation of a finite random sample?
questions.answer: Observed frequencies and statistics can differ from theoretical values.
options: It always contains invalid values.
Observed frequencies and statistics can differ from theoretical values.
It cannot be reproduced with a seed.
It must have a normal distribution.
questions.explanation: Finite samples naturally vary around theoretical expectations.
